title: Measure-Theoretic Foundations
summary: Up to now we have used probability spaces $(\Omega,\F,\Prob)$, random variables, expectations and conditional expectations, and we have occasionally deferred a technical point to this chapter. Here we collect and prove those points: why $\sigma$-algebras…

intro.x: Up to now we have used probability spaces $(\Omega,\F,\Prob)$, random variables, expectations and conditional expectations, and we have occasionally deferred a technical point to this chapter. Here we collect and prove those points: why $\sigma$-algebras are needed, what a random variable is, how expectation is defined as an integral, the three convergence theorems (monotone, Fatou, dominated), Fubini’s theorem, independence and Kolmogorov’s $0$–$1$ law, the existence of independent sequences, the characteristic function theorems (inversion, uniqueness, L'evy continuity), and the rigorous definition of conditional expectation.

The chapter assumes the real-analysis background of sequences, limits and suprema; where a deep external theorem is needed (Carath'eodory’s extension theorem, Helly’s selection theorem, the Riesz representation theorem), it is stated and clearly marked as cited.

blocks.x: Recall (Chapter 2) that a $\sigma$-algebra $\F$ on $\Omega$ contains $\Omega$ and is closed under complements and countable unions. The intersection of any collection of $\sigma$-algebras on $\Omega$ is again a $\sigma$-algebra. Hence for any collection $\mathcal C$ of subsets there is a smallest $\sigma$-algebra containing it, the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\mathcal C$, written $\sigma(\mathcal C)$ (the intersection of all $\sigma$-algebras containing $\mathcal C$).

The Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal B(\R)$ is generated by the open sets of $\R$. Equivalently it is generated by the intervals $(-\infty,x]$, $x\in\R$ (every open set is a countable union of open intervals, and each open interval $(a,b)$ is obtained from half-lines by countable unions, intersections and complements).

Let $(\Omega,\F)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be measurable spaces. A function $f:\Omega\to E$ is measurable if $f^{-1}(B)\in\F$ for every $B\in\mathcal E$. A random variable is a measurable function $X:(\Omega,\F)\to(\R,\mathcal B(\R))$. A random vector is a measurable map into $(\R^d,\mathcal B(\R^d))$.

$f$ is measurable iff $f^{-1}(C)\in\F$ for all $C$ in a collection $\mathcal C$ that generates $\mathcal E$. In particular $X:\Omega\to\R$ is a random variable iff $\{X\le x\}\in\F$ for every $x$ (the definition used in Chapter 4).
Compositions of measurable functions are measurable; continuous functions $\R\to\R$ are Borel measurable.

If $X,Y$ are random variables and $c\in\R$, then $X+Y$, $XY$, $cX$, $\max(X,Y)$ are random variables; if $X_n$ are random variables then $\sup_nX_n$, $\inf_nX_n$, $\limsup X_n$, $\liminf X_n$ are random variables (possibly $\pm\infty$), and $\{X_n\text{ converges}\}\in\F$.

(i) The collection $\{B\in\mathcal E:f^{-1}(B)\in\F\}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra (preimages commute with complements and unions) containing $\mathcal C$, hence contains $\sigma(\mathcal C)=\mathcal E$. (ii) Preimages of preimages; the preimage of an open set under a continuous function is open. (iii) $\{X+Y<c\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\{X<q\}\cap\{Y<c-q\}$ is a countable union of events; the other cases are similar. $\{\sup X_n\le x\}=\bigcap_n\{X_n\le x\}$, $\liminf X_n=\sup_n\inf_{m\ge n}X_m$, and $\{X_n\text{ converges}\}=\{\liminf X_n=\limsup X_n\}$.

For a random variable $X$, $\sigma(X)=\{X^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal B(\R)\}$ is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra making $X$ measurable; it represents “the information in $X$”. The law (or distribution) of $X$ is the probability measure $\mu_X(B)=\Prob(X\in B)$ on $(\R,\mathcal B(\R))$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: measurability is a statement about information

blocks.x: A function $Z$ is $\sigma(X)$-measurable iff $Z=g(X)$ for some Borel function $g$ (the Doob–Dynkin lemma, cited). So a random variable is determined by $X$ exactly when it is a function of $X$. This is the precise meaning of “$\F_n$ is the information in $X_1,\dots,X_n$” (Chapter 14) and of “determined by $X_1,\dots,X_n$”.

sections.title: Measures, the $\pi$–$\lambda$ theorem, and the Vitali set

blocks.x: A measure on $(\Omega,\F)$ is a function $\mu:\F\to[0,\infty]$ with $\mu(\emptyset)=0$ and countable additivity for disjoint sets. It is finite if $\mu(\Omega)<\infty$, a probability measure if $\mu(\Omega)=1$, and $\sigma$-finite if $\Omega=\bigcup_n\Omega_n$ with $\mu(\Omega_n)<\infty$.

The properties of Chapter 2 (monotonicity, countable subadditivity, continuity from below, and from above when $\mu$ is finite) hold for measures with the same proofs. The basic example beyond probability is Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ on $\R$, the unique measure on $\mathcal B(\R)$ with $\lambda((a,b])=b-a$. Its existence is Carath'eodory’s extension theorem (cited): a countably additive function on an algebra of sets extends to the generated $\sigma$-algebra, and uniquely if $\sigma$-finite.
There is no countably additive, translation-invariant measure $\lambda$ on all subsets of $[0,1)$ with $\lambda([0,1))=1$. Hence a $\sigma$-algebra strictly smaller than $2^{[0,1)}$ is unavoidable.

Suppose $\lambda$ exists, with translation understood modulo $1$ (so that translation preserves $[0,1)$). Define $x\sim y$ if $x-y\in\mathbb Q$; this is an equivalence relation on $[0,1)$. By the axiom of choice there is a set $V$ containing exactly one point of each equivalence class. For each rational $q\in[0,1)$ let $V_q=V+q\pmod1$. The sets $V_q$ are pairwise disjoint (a common point would put two points of $V$ in one class) and their union is $[0,1)$ (every $x$ is equivalent to some $v\in V$, so $x=v+q$ for some rational $q$ modulo $1$). Translation invariance gives $\lambda(V_q)=\lambda(V)=c$ for all $q$, so by countable additivity $1=\sum_{q}c$, which is $0$ if $c=0$ and $\infty$ if $c>0$. Contradiction.

A collection $\mathcal P$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is a $\pi$-system if it is closed under finite intersections. A collection $\mathcal L$ is a $\lambda$-system if (i) $\Omega\in\mathcal L$, (ii) $A,B\in\mathcal L$ and $A\subseteq B$ imply $B\setminus A\in\mathcal L$, and (iii) increasing unions of members of $\mathcal L$ are in $\mathcal L$.
If $\mathcal P$ is a $\pi$-system, $\mathcal L$ a $\lambda$-system, and $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal L$, then $\sigma(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal L$.

Let $\ell(\mathcal P)$ be the smallest $\lambda$-system containing $\mathcal P$ (the intersection of all of them). It suffices to show $\ell(\mathcal P)$ is a $\sigma$-algebra, since then $\sigma(\mathcal P)\subseteq\ell(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal L$. A $\lambda$-system is closed under complements ($A^c=\Omega\setminus A$), so it is a $\sigma$-algebra iff it is closed under finite intersections (then finite unions follow by De Morgan, and increasing limits give countable unions).

For $A\in\mathcal P$ let $\mathcal L_A=\{B:A\cap B\in\ell(\mathcal P)\}$. It is a $\lambda$-system ($A\cap\Omega=A$; if $B_1\subseteq B_2$ in $\mathcal L_A$ then $A\cap(B_2\setminus B_1)=(A\cap B_2)\setminus(A\cap B_1)$; increasing unions are preserved) and contains $\mathcal P$ (as $\mathcal P$ is a $\pi$-system). So $\mathcal L_A\supseteq\ell(\mathcal P)$: $A\cap B\in\ell(\mathcal P)$ for $A\in\mathcal P$, $B\in\ell(\mathcal P)$. Now for $B\in\ell(\mathcal P)$ let $\mathcal L_B'=\{A:A\cap B\in\ell(\mathcal P)\}$, again a $\lambda$-system; by the first step it contains $\mathcal P$, hence contains $\ell(\mathcal P)$. Thus $\ell(\mathcal P)$ is closed under intersections.

If two probability measures agree on a $\pi$-system $\mathcal P$, they agree on $\sigma(\mathcal P)$. In particular, a probability measure on $\mathcal B(\R)$ is determined by its CDF (the half-lines $(-\infty,x]$ form a $\pi$-system generating $\mathcal B(\R)$); and the law of a random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is determined by the joint CDF.

The collection of events on which the measures agree contains $\Omega$, is closed under proper differences (subtract probabilities) and increasing unions (continuity from below), so it is a $\lambda$-system containing $\mathcal P$. Apply Theorem 15.8.
This corollary justifies the claim, used throughout, that the CDF determines the distribution.
For a measure space $(\Omega,\F,\mu)$ and $f\ge0$ measurable, the integral is built in three stages.
A simple function is $s=\sum_{i=1}^ma_i\indic_{A_i}$ with $a_i\ge0$ and $A_i\in\F$ disjoint; define $\int s\,d\mu=\sum_ia_i\mu(A_i)$ (independent of the representation).
For measurable $f\ge0$, $\int f\,d\mu=\sup\bigl\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s\text{ simple},\,s\le f\bigr\}\in[0,\infty]$.

For general $f$ write $f=f^+-f^-$ with $f^\pm=\max(\pm f,0)$. If $\int f^+<\infty$ and $\int f^-<\infty$ (equivalently $\int\abs f<\infty$), $f$ is integrable and $\int f\,d\mu=\int f^+d\mu-\int f^-d\mu$.

For a random variable $X$ on $(\Omega,\F,\Prob)$, $\Exp[X]:=\int X\,d\Prob$. For the discrete and density cases of earlier chapters this agrees with the sums and integrals defined there (Theorem 15.14 below). Monotonicity ($f\le g\Rightarrow\int f\le\int g$) and $\int cf=c\int f$ for $c\ge0$ follow directly from Stage 2.
If $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\dots$ are measurable and $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$.

Monotonicity gives $\int f_n\le\int f_{n+1}\le\int f$, so $L=\lim\int f_n\le\int f$. For the reverse, let $s\le f$ be simple and $0<c<1$. The sets $E_n=\{f_n\ge cs\}$ increase to $\Omega$ (if $s(\omega)=0$ trivially; if $s(\omega)>0$ then $cs(\omega)<s(\omega)\le f(\omega)$ and $f_n(\omega)\uparrow f(\omega)$). Then $\int f_n\ge\int f_n\indic_{E_n}\ge c\int s\indic_{E_n} =c\sum_ia_i\mu(A_i\cap E_n)\to c\sum_ia_i\mu(A_i)=c\int s$ by continuity of measure from below. So $L\ge c\int s$; let $c\uparrow1$ and take the supremum over $s$.

If $f,g$ are integrable and $a,b\in\R$ then $af+bg$ is integrable and $\int(af+bg)=a\int f+b\int g$. In particular, for random variables, $\Exp[aX+bY]=a\Exp[X]+b\Exp[Y]$ whenever $X,Y$ are integrable.

For simple functions additivity is clear. For measurable $f,g\ge0$, choose simple $s_n\uparrow f$, $t_n\uparrow g$ (e.g. $s_n=\min(n,2^{-n}\lfloor2^nf\rfloor)$). Then $s_n+t_n\uparrow f+g$ and by the MCT $\int(f+g)=\lim\int(s_n+t_n)=\lim\bigl(\int s_n+\int t_n\bigr)=\int f+\int g$. For integrable $f,g$ of any sign, $(f+g)^++f^-+g^-=(f+g)^-+f^++g^+$; integrate both sides using additivity for non-negative functions and rearrange (all terms are finite). Scalar multiples are handled by $\int cf=c\int f$ for $c\ge0$ and $\int(-f)=-\int f$.
If $f_n\ge0$ are measurable then $\int\liminf f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf\int f_n\,d\mu$.
Let $g_n=\inf_{k\ge n}f_k$. Then $0\le g_n\uparrow\liminf f_n$ and $g_n\le f_k$ for $k\ge n$, so $\int g_n\le\inf_{k\ge n}\int f_k$. By MCT, $\int\liminf f_n=\lim\int g_n\le\liminf\int f_n$.
If $f_n\to f$ pointwise (or almost everywhere), and $\abs{f_n}\le g$ for an integrable $g$, then $f$ is integrable and $\int f_n\to\int f$; in fact $\int\abs{f_n-f}\to0$.

Apply Fatou to $g-f_n\ge0$ and $g+f_n\ge0$: $\int(g-f)\le\liminf\int(g-f_n)=\int g-\limsup\int f_n$ and $\int(g+f)\le\int g+\liminf\int f_n$. Subtracting the (finite) $\int g$ gives $\limsup\int f_n\le\int f\le\liminf\int f_n$. For the last claim apply the first to $\abs{f_n-f}\le2g$.

If $X$ has law $\mu_X$ and $g:\R\to\R$ is Borel with $g\ge0$ or $g(X)$ integrable, then $\Exp[g(X)]=\int_\R g\,d\mu_X$. If $\mu_X$ has density $f$ with respect to Lebesgue measure then $\Exp[g(X)]=\int g(x)f(x)\,dx$, and if $X$ is discrete, $\Exp[g(X)]=\sum_xg(x)p_X(x)$.

For $g=\indic_B$: $\Exp[\indic_B(X)]=\Prob(X\in B)=\mu_X(B)=\int\indic_Bd\mu_X$. By linearity the formula holds for simple $g$, by MCT for $g\ge0$ (take simple $g_n\uparrow g$), and by splitting $g=g^+-g^-$ in general. The density and discrete forms are the special cases $d\mu_X=f\,dx$ and $\mu_X=\sum p_X(x)\delta_x$.

A property holds almost surely (a.s.) if the exceptional set has probability zero. If $f\ge0$ and $\int f=0$ then $f=0$ a.s. (since $\mu(f>1/n)\le n\int f=0$). Changing a function on a null set does not change its integral. $L^p$ denotes the space of random variables with $\Exp\abs X^p<\infty$ (modulo almost sure equality).

Let $(\Omega_1,\F_1,\mu_1)$, $(\Omega_2,\F_2,\mu_2)$ be $\sigma$-finite measure spaces and $\mu_1\otimes\mu_2$ the product measure on $\F_1\otimes\F_2=\sigma(A\times B)$, satisfying $(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)(A\times B)=\mu_1(A)\mu_2(B)$. For a measurable $f:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\to\R$:
(Tonelli) if $f\ge0$ then $\int\!\!\int f\,d\mu_2\,d\mu_1=\int\!\!\int f\,d\mu_1\,d\mu_2=\int f\,d(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)$;
(Fubini) if $\int\abs f\,d(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)<\infty$ the same equalities hold.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the class of sets $C\in\F_1\otimes\F_2$ for which $x\mapsto\mu_2(C_x)$ is measurable (where $C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}$) and $\int\mu_2(C_x)d\mu_1(x)=(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)(C)$. It contains the rectangles $A\times B$, a $\pi$-system generating $\F_1\otimes\F_2$, and it is a $\lambda$-system: closed under proper differences and increasing unions (by linearity and the MCT). By Theorem 15.8, $\mathcal D=\F_1\otimes\F_2$, so (i) holds for indicators, hence for simple functions by linearity, and for $f\ge0$ by the MCT. (The $\sigma$-finite case follows by exhausting $\Omega_i$ with finite-measure sets, and the other order of integration is symmetric.) For (ii) apply (i) to $f^+$ and $f^-$.

Sub-$\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal G_1,\mathcal G_2,\dots\subseteq\F$ are independent if $\Prob(G_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap G_{i_k})=\prod_j\Prob(G_{i_j})$ for all distinct indices and $G_i\in\mathcal G_i$. Random variables are independent iff the $\sigma$-algebras $\sigma(X_i)$ are. Events are independent iff their indicator $\sigma$-algebras are.

If $\mathcal P_1,\mathcal P_2$ are $\pi$-systems with $\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)\Prob(B)$ for all $A\in\mathcal P_1$, $B\in\mathcal P_2$, then $\sigma(\mathcal P_1)$ and $\sigma(\mathcal P_2)$ are independent. Consequently random variables $X,Y$ are independent iff $\Prob(X\le x,Y\le y)=\Prob(X\le x)\Prob(Y\le y)$ for all $x,y$, and iff the joint law is the product law $\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y$.

Fix $A\in\mathcal P_1$. The class of $B$ with $\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)\Prob(B)$ is a $\lambda$-system containing $\mathcal P_2$, hence contains $\sigma(\mathcal P_2)$. Now fix $B\in\sigma(\mathcal P_2)$ and repeat for the class of $A$. The statement about CDFs takes the $\pi$-systems of half-lines. The joint law and $\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y$ agree on the rectangles $(-\infty,x]\times(-\infty,y]$ and hence everywhere by Corollary 15.9.
If $X,Y$ are independent and integrable (or non-negative), then $\Exp[XY]=\Exp[X]\Exp[Y]$, and $f(X),g(Y)$ are independent for Borel $f,g$.

The independence of $f(X)$ and $g(Y)$ holds since $\sigma(f(X))\subseteq\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(g(Y))\subseteq\sigma(Y)$. Let $X,Y\ge0$. The law of $(X,Y)$ is $\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y$, so by Theorem 15.14 and Tonelli, $\Exp[XY]=\iint xy\,d\mu_X(x)d\mu_Y(y)=\int x\,d\mu_X\int y\,d\mu_Y$. For general integrable $X,Y$ split into positive and negative parts and use Fubini and linearity.
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be independent random variables and let $\mathcal T=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\sigma(X_n,X_{n+1},\dots)$ be the tail $\sigma$-algebra. Then every $A\in\mathcal T$ has $\Prob(A)\in\{0,1\}$.

Fix $n$. By independence, $\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is independent of $\sigma(X_{n+1},X_{n+2},\dots)\supseteq\mathcal T$ (the independence of $\sigma$-algebras generated by disjoint groups of independent variables follows from Proposition 15.18 applied to $\pi$-systems of finite-dimensional events). So $A\in\mathcal T$ is independent of $\bigcup_n\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_n)$, a $\pi$-system that generates $\sigma(X_1,X_2,\dots)$. By Proposition 15.18, $A$ is independent of $\sigma(X_1,X_2,\dots)$. But $A$ itself lies in this $\sigma$-algebra, so $\Prob(A)=\Prob(A\cap A)=\Prob(A)^2$, whence $\Prob(A)\in\{0,1\}$.

Events such as $\{\sum X_n\text{ converges}\}$, $\{X_n\text{ converges}\}$, $\{\limsup S_n/n>c\}$ and $\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}$ (for independent events $A_n$) are tail events: changing finitely many $X_n$ does not affect them. So each has probability $0$ or $1$. This explains the all-or-nothing behaviour in the Borel–Cantelli lemmas, and shows that a random series either converges almost surely or diverges almost surely. The law does not tell which: that is the role of Kolmogorov’s three-series theorem (cited).
Existence of independent sequences
All results about i.i.d. sequences presuppose that such sequences exist on some probability space. Here is a self-contained construction.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: An i.i.d. sequence from one uniform variable

blocks.x: On $\Omega=[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure there exist independent random variables $U_1,U_2,\dots$, each uniform on $[0,1)$. Consequently for any distribution functions $F_1,F_2,\dots$ there are independent $X_j=F_j^{-1}(U_j)$ with CDF $F_j$.

For $\omega\in[0,1)$ write its binary expansion $\omega=\sum_{k\ge1}\epsilon_k(\omega)2^{-k}$ (non-terminating expansions excluded). Each $\epsilon_k$ is measurable, and for any pattern $(e_1,\dots,e_n)\in\{0,1\}^n$ the set $\{\epsilon_1=e_1,\dots,\epsilon_n=e_n\}$ is an interval of length $2^{-n}$. Hence the $\epsilon_k$ are i.i.d. Bernoulli$(\tfrac12)$. Choose a bijection $\sigma:\N\times\N\to\N$ and set $U_j=\sum_{i\ge1}\epsilon_{\sigma(i,j)}2^{-i}$. The $U_j$ are functions of disjoint sub-families of independent bits, hence independent (by Proposition 15.18 on cylinder events), and each $U_j$ has the same law as $\sum_i\epsilon_i2^{-i}$, which is uniform because $\Prob(U_j\in[m2^{-n},(m+1)2^{-n}))=2^{-n}$ for all dyadic intervals, and dyadic intervals form a $\pi$-system generating the Borel sets (Corollary 15.9). The last claim is Theorem 7.14 (and the quantile remark).
(For arbitrary joint laws on infinite product spaces one uses Kolmogorov’s extension theorem, cited.)

sections.title: Absolutely continuous laws, Radon–Nikodym and the structure of distributions

blocks.x: $ u$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$, written $ u\ll\mu$, if $\mu(A)=0$ implies $ u(A)=0$.

Let $\mu,
u$ be finite measures on $(\Omega,\F)$ with $
u\ll\mu$. Then there is a measurable $h\ge0$, unique $\mu$-a.e., with $
u(A)=\int_Ah\,d\mu$ for all $A\in\F$. We write $h=d
u/d\mu$.

Let $ho=\mu+
u$. The map $\ell(f)=\int f\,d
u$ is a bounded linear functional on $L^2(ho)$ since $\abs{\int f\,d
u}\le\int\abs f\,dho\le\sqrt{ho(\Omega)}
orm f_{L^2(ho)}$. By the Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert spaces (cited) there is $g\in L^2(ho)$ with $\int f\,d
u=\int fg\,dho$ for all $f\in L^2(ho)$. Testing with $f=\indic_{\{g<0\}}$ and $f=\indic_{\{g>1\}}$ shows $0\le g\le1$ $ho$-a.e. Rewriting, $\int f(1-g)\,d
u=\int fg\,d\mu$. Take $f=\indic_{\{g=1\}}$: $0=\mu(g=1)$, hence $
u(g=1)=0$ since $
u\ll\mu$. On $\{g<1\}$ put $h=g/(1-g)$; for $f=\indic_A/(1-g)$ (truncated and passed to the limit by the MCT) we obtain $
u(A)=\int_Ah\,d\mu$. Uniqueness: if $\int_Ah_1d\mu=\int_Ah_2d\mu$ for all $A$, take $A=\{h_1>h_2\}$ and $\{h_1<h_2\}$ to see both have $\mu$-measure $0$.
When $\nu=\mu_X$ is the law of $X$ and $\mu$ is Lebesgue measure, $h$ is exactly the density of Chapter 7; when $\mu$ is counting measure on a countable set, $h$ is the PMF.

Every distribution function $F$ on $\R$ decomposes as $F=\alpha_dF_d+\alpha_{ac}F_{ac}+\alpha_sF_s$ with non-negative weights summing to $1$, where $F_d$ is the CDF of a discrete law (atoms), $F_{ac}$ has a density, and $F_s$ is continuous but singular (concentrated on a Lebesgue null set, like the Cantor distribution). (Cited.)
This is the complete classification promised in Chapter 7: discrete, absolutely continuous, and mixtures, together with the exotic singular continuous part.
Recall $\varphi_X(t)=\Exp[e^{itX}]$. We prove the cited statements of Theorem 9.14.

If $\Exp\abs X^k<\infty$ then $\varphi_X$ is $k$ times continuously differentiable and $\varphi_X^{(k)}(0)=i^k\Exp[X^k]$. If $\Exp[X^2]<\infty$ then $\varphi_X(t)=1+it\Exp[X]-\tfrac12t^2\Exp[X^2]+o(t^2)$.

Differentiating $e^{itX}$ $k$ times in $t$ gives $(iX)^ke^{itX}$, bounded in modulus by $\abs X^k$, which is integrable. By dominated convergence (differences quotients are bounded by $\abs X^k$ via the mean value theorem), differentiation under the expectation is permitted, giving $\varphi^{(k)}(t)=\Exp[(iX)^ke^{itX}]$, continuous in $t$ by dominated convergence again. Set $t=0$. The expansion is Taylor’s theorem for $\varphi$ at $0$ with Peano remainder.
Let $F$ be the CDF of $X$ and $\varphi$ its characteristic function. For $a<b$ continuity points of $F$,
F(b)-F(a)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-T}^T\frac{e^{-ita}-e^{-itb}}{it}\,\varphi(t)\,dt .
Consequently $\varphi$ determines the distribution of $X$. If $\int\abs{\varphi(t)}dt<\infty$, then $X$ has a bounded continuous density $f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int e^{-itx}\varphi(t)\,dt$.
The kernel $\frac{e^{-ita}-e^{-itb}}{it}=\int_a^be^{-itx}dx$ has modulus at most $b-a$. By Fubini (bounded integrand on $[-T,T]\times\Omega$),
I_T:=\int_{-T}^T\frac{e^{-ita}-e^{-itb}}{it}\varphi(t)\,dt=\Exp\Bigl[\int_{-T}^T\frac{e^{it(X-a)}-e^{it(X-b)}}{it}\,dt\Bigr].

For real $c$, $\int_{-T}^T\frac{e^{itc}}{it}dt=\int_{-T}^T\frac{\sin tc}t\,dt-i\int_{-T}^T\frac{\cos tc}t\,dt =2\,\mathrm{Si}(Tc)$ (the second integral vanishes by oddness, in the principal-value sense; the combination of the two terms is integrable at $0$), where $\mathrm{Si}(y)=\int_0^y\frac{\sin u}u\,du$ is odd, bounded, and $\mathrm{Si}(y)\to\pm\pi/2$ as $y\to\pm\infty$ (the Dirichlet integral, cited from calculus). Hence the inside of the expectation is $2[\mathrm{Si}(T(X-a))-\mathrm{Si}(T(X-b))]$, which is bounded uniformly in $T$ and converges as $T\to\infty$ to $\pi[\mathrm{sgn}(X-a)-\mathrm{sgn}(X-b)]$. This equals $2\pi$ for $a<X<b$, $0$ for $X<a$ or $X>b$, and $\pi$ when $X\in\{a,b\}$, an event of probability $0$ since $a,b$ are continuity points. By bounded convergence, $I_T\to2\pi\Prob(a<X<b)=2\pi(F(b)-F(a))$.

Uniqueness: $F$ is determined at its continuity points (a dense set), and a right-continuous function is determined by its values on a dense set. For the density: when $\varphi$ is integrable the limit is an absolutely convergent integral, so by Fubini $F(b)-F(a)=\frac1{2\pi}\int\varphi(t)\int_a^be^{-itx}dx\,dt=\int_a^bf(x)\,dx$ with $f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int e^{-itx}\varphi(t)dt$.

This completes the derivation of the Cauchy characteristic function in Example 9.16 and the uniqueness theorem for characteristic functions (and, via the same transform argument for Laplace transforms, for MGFs, which are cited in Theorem 9.5).

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Bounded continuous functions characterise convergence in distribution

blocks.x: $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$ iff $\Exp[g(X_n)]\to\Exp[g(X)]$ for every bounded continuous $g:\R\to\R$.

($\Leftarrow$) For continuity point $x$ of $F_X$ and $\epsilon>0$, let $g_\epsilon$ be $1$ on $(-\infty,x-\epsilon]$, $0$ on $[x,\infty)$, linear between, and $h_\epsilon$ the analogous function between $x$ and $x+\epsilon$. Then $g_\epsilon\le\indic_{(-\infty,x]}\le h_\epsilon$, so $\Exp g_\epsilon(X_n)\le F_n(x)\le\Exp h_\epsilon(X_n)$; letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$ gives $F_n(x)\to F(x)$.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $g$ be bounded by $B$ and continuous, and $\epsilon>0$. Choose $K$ with $\pm K$ continuity points of $F_X$ and $\Prob(\abs X>K)<\epsilon$. Since $g$ is uniformly continuous on $[-K,K]$, there is a partition $-K=x_0<\dots<x_m=K$ into continuity points of $F_X$ such that $g$ varies by less than $\epsilon$ on each piece; let $s=\sum_jg(x_j)\indic_{(x_{j-1},x_j]}$. Then $\abs{\Exp g(X_n)-\Exp s(X_n)}\le\epsilon+B\Prob(\abs{X_n}>K)$, and $\Exp s(X_n)=\sum_jg(x_j)(F_n(x_j)-F_n(x_{j-1}))\to\Exp s(X)$. Also $\Prob(\abs{X_n}>K)\to\Prob(\abs X>K)<\epsilon$. Combining the estimates for $X_n$ and $X$ gives $\limsup\abs{\Exp g(X_n)-\Exp g(X)}\le C\epsilon$ for a constant $C$ depending only on $B$.
If $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$ then $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ for every $t$.
If $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi(t)$ for every $t$ and $\varphi$ is continuous at $0$, then $\varphi$ is the characteristic function of some random variable $X$ and $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$.
(i) $x\mapsto\cos tx$ and $\sin tx$ are bounded continuous; apply Theorem 15.28.
(ii) Tightness. For $u>0$, by Fubini,

\frac1u\int_{-u}^u\bigl(1-\varphi_n(t)\bigr)dt=\Exp\Bigl[\frac1u\int_{-u}^u(1-e^{itX_n})dt\Bigr]
=\Exp\Bigl[2\Bigl(1-\frac{\sin uX_n}{uX_n}\Bigr)\Bigr]\ge\Prob\bigl(\abs{X_n}\ge2/u\bigr),

because the integrand is $\ge0$ always and $\ge2(1-\tfrac1{\abs{uX_n}})\ge1$ when $\abs{uX_n}\ge2$. Given $\epsilon>0$, continuity of $\varphi$ at $0$ with $\varphi(0)=1$ gives $u$ such that $\frac1u\int_{-u}^u\abs{1-\varphi(t)}dt<\epsilon$; since $\varphi_n\to\varphi$ pointwise and boundedly, $\frac1u\int_{-u}^u(1-\varphi_n)\to\frac1u\int_{-u}^u(1-\varphi)$. So for large $n$, $\Prob(\abs{X_n}\ge2/u)<2\epsilon$: the family is tight (no mass escapes to infinity).

Subsequences. By Helly’s selection theorem (cited), every subsequence of $(F_n)$ has a further subsequence converging at all continuity points to a function $G$ that is non-decreasing and right-continuous, and tightness ensures $G$ is a genuine CDF (limits $0$ and $1$ at $\mp\infty$). By (i) the characteristic function of $G$ is the pointwise limit $\varphi$. By uniqueness (Theorem 15.27), $G$ is the same CDF for every subsequence. A sequence all of whose subsequences have a further subsequence converging to the same limit must itself converge to that limit, so $F_n\to G$ at its continuity points.
With this, the central limit theorem proof of Chapter 11 is complete.
Let $Y$ be an integrable random variable on $(\Omega,\F,\Prob)$ and $\mathcal G\subseteq\F$ a sub-$\sigma$-algebra (“the information we are allowed to use”).

A random variable $Z=\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]$ is a conditional expectation of $Y$ given $\mathcal G$ if (i) $Z$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and integrable, and (ii) $\Exp[Y\indic_G]=\Exp[Z\indic_G]$ for every $G\in\mathcal G$. For a random variable $W$ we write $\Exp[Y\given W]=\Exp[Y\given\sigma(W)]$.
A conditional expectation exists and is unique up to almost sure equality.

Uniqueness. If $Z,Z'$ both satisfy (i)–(ii), then $A=\{Z>Z'\}\in\mathcal G$ and $\Exp[(Z-Z')\indic_A]=0$, forcing $\Prob(A)=0$ (a strictly positive function on $A$ with zero integral); similarly for $\{Z

Existence. For $Y\ge0$ define the finite measure $ u(G)=\Exp[Y\indic_G]$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal G)$. Then $ u\ll\Prob|_{\mathcal G}$ (if $\Prob(G)=0$ then $ u(G)=0$). By Radon–Nikodym (Theorem 15.24) there is a $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z=d u/d\Prob|_{\mathcal G}\ge0$ with $ u(G)=\Exp[Z\indic_G]$, which is property (ii). For general $Y$ apply this to $Y^+$ and $Y^-$ and subtract.
Let $Y,Y'$ be integrable and $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\F$.
(Linearity, monotonicity) $\Exp[aY+bY'\given\mathcal G]=a\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]+b\Exp[Y'\given\mathcal G]$; $Y\le Y'$ implies $\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]\le\Exp[Y'\given\mathcal G]$ a.s.
(Tower) $\Exp[\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]\given\mathcal H]=\Exp[Y\given\mathcal H]$; in particular $\Exp[\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]]=\Exp[Y]$.
(Taking out what is known) If $W$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $WY$ is integrable, then $\Exp[WY\given\mathcal G]=W\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]$.
(Independence) If $Y$ is independent of $\mathcal G$ then $\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]=\Exp[Y]$.
(Jensen) If $\varphi$ is convex and $\varphi(Y)$ integrable, $\varphi(\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G])\le\Exp[\varphi(Y)\given\mathcal G]$.

(i) The right-hand sides are $\mathcal G$-measurable and satisfy (ii) of the definition by linearity of expectation; uniqueness identifies them. Monotonicity: apply the defining property on $G=\{\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]>\Exp[Y'\given\mathcal G]\}$. (ii) For $H\in\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$, $\Exp[\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]\indic_H]=\Exp[Y\indic_H]$; so $\Exp[Y\given\mathcal H]$ also satisfies the defining property for $\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]$ restricted to $\mathcal H$. (iii) For $W=\indic_{G_0}$, $\Exp[\indic_{G_0}Z\indic_G]=\Exp[Z\indic_{G_0\cap G}]=\Exp[Y\indic_{G_0\cap G}]$; extend to simple $W$ by linearity, to $W\ge0$ by MCT, and to general $W$ by splitting and dominated convergence. (iv) The constant $\Exp[Y]$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $\Exp[Y\indic_G]=\Exp[Y]\Prob(G)$ by independence. (v) A convex function is the supremum of countably many affine functions $\ell_j(y)=a_jy+b_j$; $\Exp[\varphi(Y)\given\mathcal G]\ge a_j\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]+b_j$ a.s. for each $j$, and take the supremum over the countable family.

If $\Exp[Y^2]<\infty$ then $\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]$ is the unique (a.s.) minimiser of $\Exp[(Y-Z)^2]$ over $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ with $\Exp[Z^2]<\infty$, and $Y-\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]$ is orthogonal to all such $Z$: $\Exp[(Y-\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G])Z]=0$.

For bounded $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$, orthogonality is the defining property with $\indic_G$ replaced by $Z$ (linearity and MCT as in (iii) above). For square-integrable $Z$ approximate by bounded truncations $Z_n=Z\indic_{\{\abs Z\le n\}}$: $Z_n\to Z$ in $L^2$, and $\abs{\Exp[(Y-\hat Y)(Z-Z_n)]}\le\norm{Y-\hat Y}_2\norm{Z-Z_n}_2\to0$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, where $\hat Y=\Exp[Y\given\mathcal G]\in L^2$ by conditional Jensen. The Pythagorean identity $\Exp[(Y-Z)^2]=\Exp[(Y-\hat Y)^2]+\Exp[(\hat Y-Z)^2]$ then gives the minimising property. This completes the “limiting argument” invoked in the proof of Theorem 10.4.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: conditioning on a null event is conditioning on a $\sigma$-algebra

blocks.x: Every conditional expectation is a random variable measurable with respect to a $\sigma$-algebra; “$\Exp[Y\given W=w]$” is the function $g$ with $\Exp[Y\given W]=g(W)$ (Doob–Dynkin), defined only up to $\mu_W$-null sets of $w$. The Borel–Kolmogorov paradox of Chapter 10 arises because “conditioning on the great circle” means different $\sigma$-algebras (generated by longitude versus by latitude). When one needs the whole conditional law of $Y$ given $W=w$, jointly measurable in $w$, one uses a regular conditional distribution, which exists for real-valued $Y$ (cited). For discrete $W$, or jointly continuous $(Y,W)$ with $f_W>0$, it is exactly the elementary construction of Chapter 10.

A probability space $(\Omega,\F,\Prob)$ is a measure space of total mass $1$. A random variable is a measurable function, and its law is the push-forward measure on $\R$, determined by the CDF. Expectation is the Lebesgue integral. The MCT, Fatou and DCT justify exchanging limits and expectations, and Tonelli/Fubini justify exchanging integrals. Independence is the product structure of the joint law. The zero–one law shows tail events are deterministic. Conditional expectation is a $\sigma$-algebra-measurable projection. Characteristic functions encode laws uniquely and convergence in distribution as pointwise convergence of the transforms. Everything proved in earlier chapters for discrete and density-based random variables holds in this generality.
Show that $\sigma(X)$ is a $\sigma$-algebra and that $X$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable iff $\sigma(X)\subseteq\mathcal G$.
Show that the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R$ is generated by (a) the intervals $(a,b]$, (b) the half-lines $(-\infty,x]$ with $x$ rational.
Prove that a finitely additive $\mu$ on a $\sigma$-algebra with $\mu(\Omega)<\infty$ is countably additive iff it is continuous from above at $\emptyset$.
Let $X_n\ge0$ be integrable with $X_n\to0$ a.s. and $\Exp[X_n]=1$. Show that DCT fails and find where the domination condition breaks (Example 11.3(ii)).
Prove that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\Exp\abs{X_n}<\infty$ implies $\sum X_n$ converges almost surely and $\Exp[\sum X_n]=\sum\Exp[X_n]$ (apply the MCT and Fubini to counting measure).
Show that if $X,Y$ are independent with $\Exp\abs X<\infty$ then $\Exp[X\given Y]=\Exp[X]$ using the rigorous definition.
Compute the characteristic function of $U(-1,1)$ and verify the inversion formula at $x=0$.
Prove Fatou’s lemma implies the first Borel–Cantelli direction: if $\sum\Prob(A_n)<\infty$ then $\Prob(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$. (Apply the MCT to $\sum_n\indic_{A_n}$.)

(Challenge) Prove Helly’s selection theorem: every sequence of CDFs has a subsequence converging at all continuity points of a non-decreasing right-continuous limit (a diagonal argument along the rationals).
